title: Density and buoyancy
question: What are density and buoyancy?

principle.name: Density and buoyancy
principle.formulaNote: buoyant force = fluid density × volume under the surface × g: the weight of the fluid pushed aside. Density is mass ÷ volume (ρ = m ÷ V). Anything less dense than the fluid floats, with ρ_object ÷ ρ_fluid of it under the surface; anything denser sinks.
principle.idea: Density is how much mass is packed into each bit of space. A fluid pushes up on anything in it with the weight of the fluid it pushes aside, so things less dense than the fluid float and denser things sink.
principle.discovered: c. 250 BCE · Archimedes, On Floating Bodies

examples.title: Hot water floats in the geyser
examples.text: Water at 60 °C is about 1.5% lighter than at 20 °C, so hot water rises to the top of a storage geyser, right where the outlet draws from, while cold water comes in at the bottom.

examples.title: The float switch in an RO tank
examples.text: A hollow float rides up on the water in the purifier's storage tank. When the tank is full the float lifts far enough to switch the pump off.

examples.title: Why the AC is mounted high
examples.text: Air at 16 °C is about 5% denser than room air at 32 °C. From high on the wall, the cold air tumbles down and stirs the whole room; mounted low, it would pool on the floor.

examples.title: Smoke rises into the chimney
examples.text: Air over a hot pan is lighter than the air around it, so it rises in a plume at about 1 m/s. The hood only has to catch what buoyancy brings up.

examples.title: A steel ship and its Plimsoll line
examples.text: A cargo ship's hollow hull gives it an average density well below water's. Load lines on its side show how deep it may float, and it sits about 2.5% deeper in fresh water than in the sea.

examples.title: An iceberg's hidden bulk
examples.text: Ice is 0.917 g/cm³, so about 92% of an ice cube hides under fresh water, and about 90% of an iceberg under the sea.

examples.title: Diving a submarine
examples.text: A Kalvari-class submarine floats at 1,615 tonnes. Flooding its ballast tanks with about 160 tonnes of sea water makes it as dense as the sea, so it can hover or dive.

examples.title: A big breath to float
examples.text: Most people are 0.98 to 1.05 g/cm³. Filling the lungs adds about 6 litres of air, which is enough to make almost anyone float.

examples.title: The hot-air balloon
examples.text: Air at 100 °C is about 20% lighter than air at 20 °C. A 2,800 m³ envelope of it lifts 600 kg or more, and more on a cool morning.

hook: Why does a 100,000-tonne steel ship float while a nail sinks? Lower blocks of cork, ice, iron and gold into a brim-full can, load a cargo ship to its Plimsoll line, test Archimedes' crown, fly a hot-air balloon, dive a submarine and float in the Dead Sea.

explainer.title: Density and the upward push
explainer.text: Density is mass ÷ volume: water is 1 g/cm³, cork 0.24, iron 7.87, gold 19.3. A fluid pushes up with the weight of the fluid pushed aside, F = ρ × V × g. Less dense than the fluid, it floats with ρ_object ÷ ρ_fluid under the surface: 92% for ice.

explainer.title: Ships, clay and a crown
explainer.text: A steel ship floats because its hollow hull averages less than 1 g/cm³. Load lines show how deep it may sit, a little deeper in fresh water than salt. A clay lump sinks but a clay bowl floats, and silver mixed into a gold crown makes it bigger, so water pushes it up harder.

explainer.title: Floating on air
explainer.text: Air at 100 °C is 20% lighter than at 20 °C, so a balloon of it lifts hundreds of kilograms. Hot water floats to the top of a geyser, and cold AC air sinks, which is why the AC goes high on the wall.

explainer.title: Swimmers, fish and submarines
explainer.text: A big breath makes most people float. Fish tune their density with a gas-filled swim bladder, submarines with ballast tanks. Salt makes water denser until a fresh egg floats, and liquids stack by density.

explainer.title: Surprises and myths
explainer.text: Water is densest at 4 °C, so lakes freeze from the top down. The Dead Sea, 1.24 g/cm³, holds a fifth of you out of the water. Astronauts train neutrally buoyant in a 12 m pool. Heavy logs float and small nails sink, and deep water doesn't float a boat any better.

concepts.def: Mass divided by volume, in kg/m³ or g/cm³. Water is 1,000 kg/m³.
The upward push of a fluid, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
F = ρ_fluid × V_submerged × g: a body in a fluid is pushed up by the weight of the fluid it pushes aside.
The fluid an object pushes aside; for a ship, the mass of water equal to the ship's own mass.
Total mass over the total volume enclosed, air spaces included. It decides whether a ship floats.
Exactly as dense as the surrounding fluid, so it neither rises nor sinks.
Warm, lighter fluid rising and cool, denser fluid sinking, carrying heat with it.
The Plimsoll mark on a ship's side showing the deepest it may legally float.
